Let
\[
u_{ij}=\langle e_i,f_j\rangle .
\]
The matrix \(U=(u_{ij})\) is orthogonal. By changing signs of the \(f_j\)'s if needed, we may assume
\[
u_{ii}=a \quad (i=1,\dots,5),
\]
while every off-diagonal entry is still \(\pm b\).

Set
\[
x=\frac ab
\]
and write \(U=bS\). Then \(S\) has diagonal entries \(x\), off-diagonal entries \(\pm1\), and its distinct rows are orthogonal.

For two different rows \(i,j\), their dot product has the form
\[
x(s_{ij}+s_{ji})+\sum_{k\ne i,j}s_{ik}s_{jk}=0.
\]
Here \(s_{ij}+s_{ji}\in\{-2,0,2\}\), while the sum has three terms each equal to \(\pm1\), so it is one of \(\{-3,-1,1,3\}\). Since that second sum is odd, \(s_{ij}+s_{ji}\neq0\). Hence
\[
x\in\left\{\frac12,\frac32\right\}.
\]

Now rule out \(x=\frac12\). If \(x=\frac12\), then \(T=2S\) is an integer matrix with diagonal entries \(1\), off-diagonal entries \(\pm2\), and mutually orthogonal rows. Each row has squared norm
\[
1+4\cdot 2^2=17,
\]
so
\[
TT^T=17I_5.
\]
Taking determinants gives
\[
(\det T)^2=17^5,
\]
impossible because \(\det T\) is an integer but \(17^5\) is not a perfect square.

Therefore
\[
\frac ab=\frac32.
\]
Also each row of \(U\) has norm \(1\), so
\[
a^2+4b^2=1.
\]
With \(a=\frac32 b\),
\[
\frac94 b^2+4b^2=\frac{25}{4}b^2=1,
\]
so \(b=\frac25\), and therefore
\[
a=\frac35.
\]

\[
\boxed{\frac35}
\]
